=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.
exchanges.text:
## Overall assessment

**Do not accept this package as drafted.** It combines broad disclosure and deemed Buyer knowledge with limits applying to virtually every claim. That could leave Wattlebridge bearing identified risks while also losing meaningful remedies for undisclosed problems.

The immediate priorities are **Bluefen consent, Riverlark repayment and security release, ownership of the Ironquay IP, and correct treatment of Completion bonuses**. The liability provisions then need restructuring so they do not undermine those protections.

This assessment is based on the Seller’s summaries and Disclosure Letter—not the underlying DD documents, complete SPA or funds flow. Those documents must be checked before final drafting.

## 1. Liability protections: reject the blanket regime

### General warranty cap and thresholds

The proposed general warranty cap is **AUD 4.8 million (20% of price)**. Claims must individually exceed AUD 25,000, and only aggregate qualifying losses above AUD 250,000 are recoverable.

**Buyer concern:** These provisions operate cumulatively. Numerous smaller losses could be excluded entirely; even qualifying claims suffer an unrecoverable first AUD 250,000. The cap also needs assessment against the actual business risks and Seller’s ability to pay—not acceptance because it is presented as negotiated.

**Push back:**
- Seek a higher general warranty cap, informed by diligence and available recovery security.
- Reduce the de minimis and aggregate related claims so one underlying problem cannot be fragmented below the threshold.
- Seek a **tipping basket**, allowing recovery of all qualifying losses once the basket is crossed, rather than only the excess.
- Confine these thresholds and the general cap to genuinely general warranty claims.

### Fundamental warranties, tax and specific indemnities

Reject the proposal to treat title and capacity like ordinary business warranties “for administrative simplicity”.

**Reason:** Wattlebridge is paying for valid ownership of 100% of the shares. A maximum AUD 4.8 million recovery is inadequate if the Seller cannot convey that ownership.

Seek:
- Separate fundamental warranties covering Seller capacity, authority, ownership, the entire issued capital and absence of encumbrances, with a cap **at least equal to the purchase price** and a substantially longer claim period.
- A separate tax indemnity for pre-Completion taxes, appropriate tax warranties and a tax-specific limitation period aligned with assessment and recovery risks.
- Separate treatment for negotiated specific indemnities, including Ironquay and any incident indemnity—not automatic application of general caps, baskets or exclusions.
- Survival of payment obligations, purchase-price adjustments, debt discharge and other express covenants independently of general warranty limitations.

IP warranties should also be reconsidered on their merits. Calling them “settled” does not resolve the known ownership gap or establish adequate protection for an analytics business.

### Time limits and claims procedure

Eighteen months may provide too little time to uncover problems through a complete post-acquisition reporting cycle. Seek a longer general period, for example **24–36 months**, with separate longer periods for fundamental and tax claims.

Delete the rule extending every claim limitation to all Claims unless expressly excluded. Instead, specify exactly which restrictions apply to each claim category. Ensure timely notification preserves a claim while investigation or third-party proceedings continue, and avoid technical notice requirements that unnecessarily forfeit recovery.

### Exclusive remedy, non-reliance and “all Claims” limitations

Clauses 9.3, 12.8 and 20.5 could undermine protections elsewhere in the SPA.

**Push back:** Narrow their scope and preserve:
- Fraud, fraudulent misrepresentation and deliberate concealment.
- Rights that cannot lawfully be excluded.
- Express indemnities, payment and adjustment obligations, and Completion covenants.
- Appropriate termination, specific performance and injunctive relief.

Non-reliance wording should not contradict express contractual assurances or operate as a factual acknowledgement Wattlebridge cannot honestly give. Its effect on statutory claims requires review under the complete drafting; do not assume a generic carve-out solves every issue.

## 2. Disclosure and Buyer knowledge: prevent a blanket defence

The Seller seeks both wholesale disclosure of the data room/public records and a bar for anything the Buyer or its advisers knew—or could have discovered.

**Buyer concern:** This effectively transfers the risk of finding and interpreting every problem to Wattlebridge. The inclusion of a document does not necessarily explain the nature, scope or financial consequences of a warranty exception.

**Push back:**
- Require **fair, specific disclosure**, with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of each matter and its relevant warranty.
- Reject blanket disclosure of all data-room material, statutory registers and public records. Any accepted general disclosures should be narrow and clearly defined.
- Freeze and preserve the disclosed data-room index and contents. Check developments since the **22 September 2026** cut-off.
- Delete constructive knowledge and the “discoverable” standard. Resist attribution of every adviser’s knowledge; any agreed knowledge exclusion should be narrowly limited to actual knowledge of named Buyer personnel.
- State that disclosure and knowledge do **not** qualify specific indemnities, conditions precedent, price adjustments or express remediation obligations unless expressly agreed.

The Disclosure Letter identifies risks; it does not cure them. Its reservation that no liability or legal requirement is admitted does not determine the Buyer’s contractual protection.

## 3. Bluefen: make effective consent a genuine Completion condition

Bluefen represents approximately **AUD 3.6 million, or 30% of FY26 revenue**. No final consent or evidence satisfying associated conditions has been supplied.

**Buyer concern:** “Reasonable endeavours” is only an effort obligation. Delivery of a consent letter may not satisfy clause 11.3 or protect against adverse commercial conditions.

**Push back:**
- Require effective written change-of-control consent, with all associated conditions satisfied, as a condition precedent.
- Require the consent to cover this transaction and preserve the relevant contract without materially adverse amendments, fees or termination rights.
- Give Wattlebridge approval over consent terms and control over waiver of the condition.
- Include an appropriate long-stop date and termination rights.

Do not describe the issue as “addressed” until the underlying contractual requirements and consent evidence have been checked.

## 4. Riverlark: no post-Completion security-release gap

Approximately **AUD 3.2 million** remains outstanding. A release promised after Completion is inconsistent with delivering the agreed debt-free business without an unsecured discharge risk.

**Push back:**
- Obtain a current lender payout letter covering principal, accrued interest, fees and other secured obligations.
- Pay the lender directly through Completion funds flow.
- Require an effective discharge/release mechanism at Completion covering all relevant security and guarantees, with appropriate undertakings and subsequent registration evidence.
- Address the facility’s change-of-control requirements.
- Deduct debt through the agreed price mechanism, without double counting.

A later administrative registration step may be manageable under an enforceable release arrangement; a mere promise to procure release later is not equivalent.

## 5. Completion bonuses: prevent leakage into Buyer economics

The **AUD 420,000** bonuses are conditional on Completion and continued employment, and are omitted from the draft funds flow.

**Buyer concern:** Calling them “a matter for the Seller” does not stop the acquired company becoming liable after Wattlebridge owns it.

**Push back:**
- Allocate the bonuses expressly to the Seller economically, through payment at Completion or an agreed debt-like/transaction-expense deduction.
- Establish who owes them, when they crystallise and whether payroll tax, superannuation, withholding or other on-costs apply.
- Include all applicable costs and payment mechanics in the funds flow.
- Ensure consistent treatment across debt, working capital and transaction expenses, with no double counting.

AUD 420,000 is the disclosed bonus amount, **not necessarily the total exposure**.

## 6. Ironquay IP: secure ownership, not merely a payment indemnity

The disclosed transfer condition requires cleared payment of **every SOW3 fee**. AUD 180,000 is recorded as open, but the materials do not independently establish whether it remains unpaid.

**Buyer concern:** An indemnity restricted to the SOW3 payment may leave Wattlebridge without important IP and without compensation for disruption, infringement allegations or replacement costs.

**Push back:**
- Verify all SOW3 amounts and payment status.
- Require payment where outstanding and a confirmatory assignment/release establishing the Company’s rights before Completion.
- Check the relevant chain of title, personnel/subcontractor assignments, licences and third-party components.
- Broaden the specific indemnity to losses arising from the identified ownership defect or dispute, rather than just the invoice amount, with negotiated separate limitations.
- Assess whether the IP is sufficiently business-critical to make remediation a Completion condition.

Do not assume either that title has transferred or that non-payment is conclusively established.

## 7. Export/privacy incident: investigate before accepting reassurance

The evidence describes a link sent to an unintended external address, potentially exposing approximately **1,240 records**. Access, scope and notification requirements remain unresolved.

**Buyer concern:** Neither “preliminary” nor the absence of quantified loss establishes immateriality. Equally, the documents do not establish a confirmed notifiable breach.

**Push back:**
- Obtain the investigation evidence: link permissions, access/download logs, revocation timing, data scope, recipient response and containment steps.
- Assess applicable privacy, contractual and regulatory obligations, including notification requirements.
- Require prompt updates, evidence preservation and agreed remediation covenants.
- Seek a specific indemnity for the pre-Completion incident, with appropriate control of investigations and third-party claims.
- Consider a holdback or Completion condition if the unresolved risk is sufficiently serious.

Do not let general disclosure extinguish protection for this known incident.

## 8. Sandbar renewals: assess the combined commitment

Three related renewals total **AUD 330,000**. Neither “ordinary course” nor an automatic price deduction is established.

**Push back:** Review them together for renewal dates, duration, cancellation rights, commercial necessity, pricing and payment status. Test aggregate commitments against interim operating covenants and Buyer-consent thresholds. Determine whether amounts are ordinary future operating expenditure, accrued liabilities, prepayments or exceptional commitments before deciding price treatment.

## 9. Lease, Mossvale and title: require the right evidence

- **Office lease:** The disclosed obligation is notification, not landlord consent. Confirm timing and compliance; require notice evidence rather than inventing a consent condition.
- **Mossvale:** An assignment restriction does not itself mean a share sale requires consent. Review the complete agreement for change-of-control, deemed-assignment and termination provisions.
- **Share title:** DD-012 is relevant evidence, not complete verification. Reconcile the register with corporate records, issuance and transfer documents; check options, convertibles, other equity rights and encumbrances. Require appropriate title warranties and valid Completion transfers and registrations.

## Recommended negotiating position

| Priority | Buyer requirement |
|---|---|
| **Completion-critical** | Effective Bluefen consent; Riverlark payout and release; verified Ironquay ownership/remediation; correct bonus funding and price treatment. |
| **Core contractual protection** | Separate fundamental, tax and specific-indemnity regimes; narrow “all Claims” provisions; stronger general warranty protection. |
| **Disclosure protection** | Fair, specific disclosure; no deemed discoverability; no disclosure/knowledge defence against agreed specific protections. |
| **Risk resolution** | Investigate the export incident; evaluate Sandbar commitments collectively; complete title and contractual diligence. |
| **Recovery security** | Assess Seller creditworthiness and negotiate an escrow, retention or other support proportionate to unresolved exposure. |

**Bottom line:** Make known risks subject to concrete closing deliverables, price treatment or targeted indemnities. Do not accept a structure where the Seller discloses a problem, promises limited efforts to address it, and then relies on broad exclusions to leave Wattlebridge with the consequences.
